caseStudies.title: Compute nodes that register themselves
caseStudies.summary: On-demand autoscaling for backup jobs, where every new node has to find its own way home.
caseStudies.problem: Backup jobs ran on a fixed pool of compute, so big jobs queued up and idle machines still cost money. New nodes could not simply be added: their IP addresses are unknown in advance and the network to the control server only works in one direction.
caseStudies.approach: I designed nodes that spin up on demand from machine images kept current, then register themselves with the control server. Each node runs with least-privilege IAM permissions, reaches only the databases it needs, and trusts controller nodes that live in a separate AWS account.
caseStudies.result: Jobs finish faster because compute grows with the queue, and nodes shut down when the work is done, so compute is only paid for while it is used.

caseStudies.title: One product, six cloud databases
caseStudies.summary: Backup and restore for managed databases across AWS and Azure.
caseStudies.problem: Every managed database exposes different APIs, limits and failure modes, but customers expect protection to behave the same way everywhere.
caseStudies.approach: I built and hardened backup and restore support for Oracle on AWS, DynamoDB, Redshift, DocumentDB, RDS and MSSQL / Azure SQL inside one product, and automated the verification that used to be done by hand.
caseStudies.result: Six database services protected under a single workflow, with automated checks replacing manual verification.

caseStudies.title: Teaching an AI to add new SaaS backups
caseStudies.summary: A faster route to supporting new SaaS applications.
caseStudies.problem: Supporting each new SaaS application meant writing custom integration code, which made every new workload slow to ship.
caseStudies.approach: I worked on an AI-assisted approach, where a trained model does much of the per-application work. The BigCommerce agent was one of the workloads delivered this way.
caseStudies.result: New SaaS workloads could be added much faster than with hand-written integrations.
